title: Complex numbers and the Argand diagram
summary: A [[complex-number|complex number]] $z = a + b\mathrm{i}$ uses a new number $\mathrm{i}$, whose square is $-1$, so every quadratic has roots. You read off its parts, [[complex-conjugate|conjugate]], [[complex-modulus|modulus]] and [[complex-argument|argument]], and plot it as a point on an [[argand-diagram|Argand diagram]].

goals.text: Use $\mathrm{i}^{2} = -1$ to write roots of negative numbers and of quadratics as $a + b\mathrm{i}$.
Read off the [[real-part|real part]], the [[imaginary-part|imaginary part]] and the [[complex-conjugate|conjugate]], and equate parts.
Plot [[complex-number|complex numbers]] and their conjugates as points on an [[argand-diagram|Argand diagram]].
Find the [[complex-modulus|modulus]] and the [[complex-argument|argument]], with the angle in the right quadrant.

before.prompt: How many real roots does $2x^{2} - 3x + 4 = 0$ have?
before.hint: Work out $\Delta = b^{2} - 4ac$ and look at its sign.
before.explain: $\Delta = (-3)^{2} - 4(2)(4) = 9 - 32 = -23$. That is negative, so there are no real roots. Revise it in {{lesson:2.7}}.

before.hint: Use $\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ with the exact values you know.

sections.heading: The number i and Cartesian form

blocks.text: No real number squared is negative, so $x^{2} = -9$ has no real solution. In {{lesson:2.7}} this was the case $\Delta < 0$: no real roots.
So mathematicians added one new number, $\mathrm{i}$, whose square is $-1$. Then $x = \pm 3\mathrm{i}$, because $(3\mathrm{i})^{2} = 9\mathrm{i}^{2} = -9$.

blocks.statement: The imaginary unit $\mathrm{i}$ is the number with $\mathrm{i}^{2} = -1$. For a positive real number $k$, $\sqrt{-k} = \sqrt{k}\,\mathrm{i}$.
blocks.plain: i is a number whose square is minus one.

blocks.statement: A [[complex-number|complex number]] in [[cartesian-form|Cartesian form]] is $z = a + b\mathrm{i}$, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The set of all complex numbers is $\mathbb{C}$.
blocks.plain: A complex number is a real number plus a real multiple of i.

blocks.text: This form is in the formula booklet. A real number is a complex number with $b = 0$. A number such as $4\mathrm{i}$, with $a = 0$, is purely imaginary.

Powers of $\mathrm{i}$ repeat every four: $\mathrm{i}^{1} = \mathrm{i}$, $\mathrm{i}^{2} = -1$, $\mathrm{i}^{3} = -\mathrm{i}$, $\mathrm{i}^{4} = 1$. For a higher power, divide by $4$ and use the remainder.

blocks.question: Write $3 - \sqrt{-20}$ in the form $a + b\mathrm{i}$.
steps: Take out the minus sign as $\mathrm{i}$: $\sqrt{-20} = \sqrt{20}\,\mathrm{i}$.
Simplify the surd: $\sqrt{20} = \sqrt{4 \times 5} = 2\sqrt{5}$.
So $3 - \sqrt{-20} = 3 - 2\sqrt{5}\,\mathrm{i}$. Here $a = 3$ and $b = -2\sqrt{5}$, and both are real, as they must be.

blocks.text: Writing $\sqrt{-16} = -4$. No real number squares to $-16$, so the answer must contain $\mathrm{i}$: $\sqrt{-16} = 4\mathrm{i}$.
With $\mathrm{i}$, the quadratic formula works even when $\Delta < 0$.

blocks.question: Solve $z^{2} - 6z + 13 = 0$, giving your answers in the form $a + b\mathrm{i}$.
steps: The coefficients are $1$, $-6$ and $13$. The discriminant is $\Delta = (-6)^{2} - 4(1)(13) = 36 - 52 = -16$.
$\Delta < 0$, so there are no real roots. Its square root is $\sqrt{-16} = 4\mathrm{i}$.
Use the quadratic formula: $z = \frac{6 \pm 4\mathrm{i}}{2}$.
Divide both the [[real-part|real part]] and the [[imaginary-part|imaginary part]] by $2$: $z = 3 \pm 2\mathrm{i}$.
Check one root. $(3 + 2\mathrm{i})^{2} = 9 + 12\mathrm{i} + 4\mathrm{i}^{2} = 5 + 12\mathrm{i}$. Then $(5 + 12\mathrm{i}) - 6(3 + 2\mathrm{i}) + 13 = (5 - 18 + 13) + (12 - 12)\mathrm{i} = 0$.

blocks.text: The two roots differ only in the sign of the imaginary part. This always happens when the coefficients are real. You will see why in {{lesson:1.14}}.

blocks.hint: Divide $30$ by $4$. What is the remainder?
Find $\Delta$ first, then write $\sqrt{\Delta}$ as a real multiple of $\mathrm{i}$.
blocks.explain: $\Delta = 16 - 116 = -100$, so $\sqrt{\Delta} = 10\mathrm{i}$. Then $z = \frac{-4 \pm 10\mathrm{i}}{2} = -2 \pm 5\mathrm{i}$. Divide the imaginary part by $2$ as well.

sections.heading: Real part, imaginary part and conjugate

blocks.text: A [[complex-number|complex number]] $z = a + b\mathrm{i}$ is built from two real numbers, $a$ and $b$. Each one has a name.

blocks.statement: For $z = a + b\mathrm{i}$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{Re}(z) = a$ is the [[real-part|real part]] of $z$ and $\mathrm{Im}(z) = b$ is its [[imaginary-part|imaginary part]].
blocks.plain: The real part stands alone. The imaginary part is the real number that multiplies i.

blocks.text: Giving $\mathrm{Im}(3 - 7\mathrm{i})$ as $-7\mathrm{i}$. The imaginary part is a real number, the one that multiplies $\mathrm{i}$, so it is $-7$.

blocks.statement: The [[complex-conjugate|conjugate]] of $z = a + b\mathrm{i}$ is $z^{*} = a - b\mathrm{i}$. It has the same real part as $z$ and the opposite imaginary part.
blocks.plain: To get the conjugate, change the sign in front of the i part.

blocks.text: Write the number as $a + b\mathrm{i}$ before you read off its parts. For example, $4\mathrm{i} - 9 = -9 + 4\mathrm{i}$ has real part $-9$, not $4$.

blocks.question: Let $z = \sqrt{-18} - 2$. Find $\mathrm{Re}(z)$, $\mathrm{Im}(z)$ and $z^{*}$.
steps: Write the root with $\mathrm{i}$: $\sqrt{-18} = \sqrt{18}\,\mathrm{i} = 3\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{i}$, since $\sqrt{18} = \sqrt{9 \times 2}$.
Put the real part first: $z = -2 + 3\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{i}$.
Read off the parts: $\mathrm{Re}(z) = -2$ and $\mathrm{Im}(z) = 3\sqrt{2}$, with no $\mathrm{i}$.
Change the sign of the imaginary part to get the conjugate: $z^{*} = -2 - 3\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{i}$.

blocks.text: Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts. So one complex equation gives you two real equations.

blocks.statement: If $a + b\mathrm{i} = c + d\mathrm{i}$, where $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R}$, then $a = c$ and $b = d$.
blocks.why: Rearrange to $a - c = (d - b)\mathrm{i}$. If $d \neq b$, then $\mathrm{i} = \frac{a - c}{d - b}$ would be real, which is impossible. So $d = b$, and then $a = c$.

blocks.question: Find the real numbers $p$ and $q$ such that $(p - 2q) + (p + q)\mathrm{i} = 8 - \mathrm{i}$.
steps: Equate the real parts: $p - 2q = 8$.
Equate the imaginary parts: $p + q = -1$, since $8 - \mathrm{i} = 8 + (-1)\mathrm{i}$.
Subtract the first equation from the second: $3q = -9$, so $q = -3$. Then $p = -1 - q = 2$.

blocks.explain: $z^{*} = 6 + 5\mathrm{i}$. Its imaginary part is the real number $5$, not $5\mathrm{i}$.

blocks.prompt: Find the real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $(a + b) + (a - b)\mathrm{i} = 4 - 6\mathrm{i}$.
blocks.hint: Equate real parts, then imaginary parts.
blocks.explain: $a + b = 4$ and $a - b = -6$. Adding them gives $2a = -2$, so $a = -1$ and $b = 5$.

blocks.text: A [[complex-number|complex number]] $a + b\mathrm{i}$ is fixed by two real numbers, just as a point is fixed by its two coordinates. So you can draw every complex number as a point.

blocks.statement: An [[argand-diagram|Argand diagram]], or complex plane, has a horizontal real axis and a vertical imaginary axis. The number $z = a + b\mathrm{i}$ is shown by the point $(a, b)$.

blocks.alt: Argand diagram with a horizontal real axis labelled Re and a vertical imaginary axis labelled Im. Points are plotted at 3 plus 2i in the first quadrant, its conjugate 3 minus 2i directly below it in the fourth quadrant, minus 4 plus i in the second quadrant, minus 2 on the real axis and minus 3i on the imaginary axis. A dashed vertical line joins 3 plus 2i to 3 minus 2i, crossing the real axis halfway.
blocks.caption: Reflect $3 + 2\mathrm{i}$ in the real axis to get its [[complex-conjugate|conjugate]], $3 - 2\mathrm{i}$.

blocks.text: Real numbers sit on the real axis, because $b = 0$. Purely imaginary numbers, such as $-3\mathrm{i}$, sit on the imaginary axis, because $a = 0$.

blocks.statement: On an Argand diagram, the point $z^{*}$ is $z$ reflected in the real axis. The point $-z$ is $z$ rotated by $\pi$ about the origin.
blocks.why: For $z^{*}$, $(a, b)$ moves to $(a, -b)$. For $-z$, it moves to $(-a, -b)$.

blocks.text: Drawn as an arrow from $O$, $a + b\mathrm{i}$ behaves like the vector $\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}$ of {{lesson:3.12}}.

blocks.question: The point $(-4, 1)$ on an Argand diagram represents $z$. Write down $z^{*}$.
steps: Read across, then up: $-4$ across and $1$ up, so $z = -4 + \mathrm{i}$.
Change the sign of the imaginary part: $z^{*} = -4 - \mathrm{i}$. Its point, $(-4, -1)$, is in the third quadrant.
Answer with a complex number, not coordinates. The point only represents it.

blocks.question: Let $z = -5 + 2\mathrm{i}$. The points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ on an Argand diagram represent $z$, $z^{*}$, $-z$ and $-z^{*}$. Find the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$.
steps: Write each number: $z^{*} = -5 - 2\mathrm{i}$, $-z = 5 - 2\mathrm{i}$ and $-z^{*} = 5 + 2\mathrm{i}$.
Two sides are vertical and two are horizontal, so $ABCD$ is a rectangle.
Width $BC = 5 - (-5) = 10$ and height $AB = 2 - (-2) = 4$, so the area is $10 \times 4 = 40$.

blocks.prompt: Let $z = -2 + 5\mathrm{i}$. In which quadrant of the Argand diagram is the point for $-z^{*}$?
blocks.hint: Find $z^{*}$ first. Then change the sign of both parts.
blocks.explain: $z^{*} = -2 - 5\mathrm{i}$, so $-z^{*} = 2 + 5\mathrm{i}$. Both parts are positive: first quadrant.

blocks.prompt: A point on an Argand diagram is at $(0, -7)$. Which complex number does it represent?
blocks.hint: The first coordinate is the real part. The second is the imaginary part.
blocks.explain: Real part $0$, imaginary part $-7$: the number is $0 - 7\mathrm{i} = -7\mathrm{i}$.

blocks.text: A point can also be fixed by its distance from $O$ and its direction. For a [[complex-number|complex number]], these are its [[complex-modulus|modulus]] and its [[complex-argument|argument]].

blocks.statement: The modulus of $z = a + b\mathrm{i}$ is its distance from the origin on an [[argand-diagram|Argand diagram]]: $\lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}$.
blocks.plain: How far the point is from zero.

blocks.text: This is Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with sides $\lvert a\rvert$ and $\lvert b\rvert$. A modulus is never negative.

blocks.statement: The argument $\arg z$ of $z \neq 0$ is the angle, in radians, from the positive real axis to the line from $O$ to $z$. Anticlockwise is positive.
blocks.plain: The direction of the point, seen from zero.

blocks.text: The question states the range. Usually it is $-\pi < \arg z \le \pi$, so points below the real axis have a negative argument.

blocks.alt: Argand diagram with the point minus 4 plus 3i in the second quadrant. A line of length 5 joins the origin to the point. The angle theta is marked from the positive real axis, turning anticlockwise to this line, so it is more than a right angle. A smaller angle alpha is marked between the line and the negative real axis. Dashed lines drop from the point to minus 4 on the real axis and across to 3 on the imaginary axis.
blocks.caption: For $z = -4 + 3\mathrm{i}$: $\lvert z\rvert = 5$, $\alpha = \arctan\frac{3}{4}$ and $\arg z = \pi - \alpha$.

blocks.text: $\tan\theta = \frac{b}{a}$ alone can't fix the angle, because two angles $\pi$ apart share a tangent. So use a sketch.
1. Sketch the point and note its quadrant.
2. Find the acute angle $\alpha$ between the line from $O$ and the real axis: $\tan\alpha = \frac{\lvert b\rvert}{\lvert a\rvert}$.
3. Turn $\alpha$ into $\arg z$. First quadrant: $\alpha$. Second: $\pi - \alpha$. Third: $-(\pi - \alpha)$. Fourth: $-\alpha$.
On the axes, $\arg z$ is $0$ (right), $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (up), $\pi$ (left) or $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ (down). The number $0$ has no argument.

blocks.question: Find the modulus and argument of $z = 3 - 3\mathrm{i}$, where $-\pi < \arg z \le \pi$.
steps: Modulus: $\lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{3^{2} + (-3)^{2}} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$.
Sketch: the [[real-part|real part]] is positive and the [[imaginary-part|imaginary part]] is negative, so the point is in the fourth quadrant.
Acute angle: $\tan\alpha = \frac{3}{3} = 1$, so $\alpha = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
Below the real axis, the argument is negative: $\arg z = -\frac{\pi}{4}$.

blocks.question: Find the exact modulus and argument of $z = -\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{i}$, where $-\pi < \arg z \le \pi$.
steps: Modulus: $\lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{(-\sqrt{6})^{2} + (\sqrt{2})^{2}} = \sqrt{6 + 2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$.
Sketch: the real part is negative and the imaginary part is positive, so the point is in the second quadrant.
Acute angle: $\tan\alpha = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{6}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $\alpha = \frac{\pi}{6}$. This is an exact value from {{lesson:3.5}}.
Second quadrant: $\arg z = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}$.
Check: $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} < 0$ and $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} > 0$, matching the second quadrant.

blocks.text: Typing $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$ and stopping. For $-\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{i}$ that gives $-\frac{\pi}{6}$, a fourth-quadrant angle, but the point is in the second quadrant. Sketch first, then adjust.

blocks.statement: For any $z$ and its [[complex-conjugate|conjugate]] $z^{*}$, $zz^{*} = \lvert z\rvert^{2}$ and $\lvert z^{*}\rvert = \lvert z\rvert$.
blocks.why: Expand, using $\mathrm{i}^{2} = -1$: $(a + b\mathrm{i})(a - b\mathrm{i}) = a^{2} - ab\mathrm{i} + ab\mathrm{i} - b^{2}\mathrm{i}^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$. And $z^{*}$ is a reflection of $z$ in the real axis, so it is the same distance from $O$.

blocks.text: The reflection also flips the angle: $\arg(z^{*}) = -\arg z$, unless $z$ is a negative real number. In {{lesson:1.13}}, $zz^{*}$ being real is how you divide.

blocks.question: Use your calculator to find the modulus and argument of $z = -5 - 2\mathrm{i}$, where $-\pi < \arg z \le \pi$. Give your answers to 3 s.f.
steps: Set the calculator to radians first.
Modulus: $\lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{(-5)^{2} + (-2)^{2}} = \sqrt{29} = 5.3851\ldots$
Sketch: both parts are negative, so the point is in the third quadrant and $\arg z$ is negative.
Acute angle: $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) = 0.38050\ldots$. Keep the full value; don't round it yet.
Third quadrant: $\arg z = -(\pi - \alpha) = -2.7610\ldots$. The calculator's complex tools give both values directly.

blocks.explain: Third quadrant, $\alpha = \frac{\pi}{6}$, so $\arg z = -\left(\pi - \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{5\pi}{6}$. $\frac{7\pi}{6}$ points the same way but is outside the range.
$zz^{*} = \lvert z\rvert^{2} = 1^{2} + 4^{2} = 17$. It is real, even though $z$ is not.

blocks.text: $\mathrm{i}^{2} = -1$, so $\sqrt{-k} = \sqrt{k}\,\mathrm{i}$ for $k > 0$. Powers of $\mathrm{i}$ repeat every $4$.
$\mathrm{Re}(a + b\mathrm{i}) = a$ and $\mathrm{Im}(a + b\mathrm{i}) = b$, a real number. The conjugate is $z^{*} = a - b\mathrm{i}$.
Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts.
Argand diagram: $a + b\mathrm{i}$ is the point $(a, b)$. $z^{*}$ is its reflection in the real axis.
$\arg z$: sketch, find the acute angle $\alpha$, then use $\alpha$, $\pi - \alpha$, $-(\pi - \alpha)$ or $-\alpha$ by quadrant, in radians.

mistakes: Giving the imaginary part with an $\mathrm{i}$. $\mathrm{Im}(4 - 9\mathrm{i})$ is $-9$, the real number that multiplies $\mathrm{i}$, not $-9\mathrm{i}$.
Picking an argument in the wrong quadrant. Two angles $\pi$ apart share a tangent, so sketch the point first.
Giving an argument outside the range, such as $\frac{7\pi}{6}$ for $-\pi < \arg z \le \pi$. Subtract $2\pi$: $-\frac{5\pi}{6}$.
Leaving out the square root. $a^{2} + b^{2}$ is $\lvert z\rvert^{2}$, not $\lvert z\rvert$.
Leaving the calculator in degrees. Arguments are in radians unless the question says otherwise.
Answering with coordinates such as $(3, -1)$. Write the complex number, $3 - \mathrm{i}$.
examTips: “Find” a modulus and argument: show $\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}$ and your angle working. A quick sketch shows your quadrant.
When unknowns are given to be real, equate real parts and imaginary parts. Writing both equations shows your method.
Use exact values on Paper 1, such as $2\sqrt{2}$ and $\frac{5\pi}{6}$. On Paper 2, set radians first and give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.
